This is why the early shuyukh focused on hunger above almost everything else in their teaching. This does not mean becoming anorexic. The point is simply: learn discipline. Two meals a day is enough — I can say that with confidence. Morning and late afternoon. If you want a third, make it something light in the evening. But two genuine meals are sufficient.

There is a man mentioned — he was from Yemen, from the tribe of Bani Hanifa, actually of the Hanafi persuasion, and I cannot recall his name at this moment — who came to the Prophet, and the story is in al-Bukhari. The Prophet gave him a bowl of milk. He drank it. The Prophet asked if he wanted more. He said yes. The Prophet kept giving, bowl after bowl, until the man had drunk seven bowls. The next day he embraced Islam, and that evening when he returned, he could only manage one bowl. The Companions who had watched him drink seven the night before were astonished. They asked the Prophet about it. He said: — the disbeliever eats from seven intestines — but the believer eats from one. So actually reduces the appetite.

Now, people today eat far more than people have eaten at virtually any other point in human history. There is a massive surplus of food, driven by agribusiness. Meat consumption in particular has risen dramatically. Ask your grandparents — if they are still alive — how often they ate meat. If they were not from a wealthy family, the answer in most Muslim-majority countries was probably once a week, if they lived in a city; far less if they lived in a village. Many Yemenis, for instance, ate meat only on Eid. This is within living memory.

And in this country too, people who are older remember a time when you did not have snacks available around the clock. Children did not have constant access to food between meals. You ate when it was mealtime, and that was that. There were no convenience stores on every block selling cold drinks and packaged food at any hour. All of this is part of a modern culture that in this regard is making people behave more like animals — mentions in the Quran that such people are like cattle, simply grazing. Some of those co-op-style bulk food stores actually post signs near the open bins that say "No Grazing." That sign says something. Sociologists call it "food contact," and research suggests the average American has around twenty food contacts per day — twenty separate occasions during the day when food is consumed or handled. Some nutritionists even recommend this pattern of small, frequent eating as healthier, but if you look at traditional cultures worldwide, people ate at set times and did not eat between meals. The absence of refrigeration alone enforced much of that. A Bedouin from Mauritania can go days on very little food, because that kind of discipline has been built into his life.

As for the American military: they now have self-heating field rations — you pour in water, a chemical reaction activates, and the food is hot. They have Indian curries for Sikh soldiers, and various options for different ethnic groups, with special requests accommodated. All of this erodes fortitude. And for every one soldier in the field, seventeen support personnel are required. The plans at the time called for every soldier to eventually carry a personal PC. It is difficult to imagine an army of that kind maintaining its edge — but that is a whole other discussion.

The point is that fasting instills discipline. Muslims, from the practice of Ramadan alone, have the experience of going extended periods without food — they are used to it. The tragedy is that Ramadan itself has been compromised: Muslims now often eat more during Ramadan than in any other month. I have seen it — the night is not given to worship but to feasting, massive spreads lasting until dawn. Walimas and dinner invitations have become extravagant productions, to the point where a person feels unable to invite anyone over without preparing something elaborate. The Prophets of, peace be upon them, warned against all of this. The Prophet would sometimes host guests with dates and water. You do not have to go that far, but when you are a guest, be content with whatever is served and do not take it as an insult if the spread is modest. If someone keeps things simple, assume the best — perhaps they are following the., a good opinion of people, is always the wiser path. You never lose by assuming the best.

So, regarding hunger — there is much more that could be said, but practically speaking: if food is something you struggle to discipline yourself around, begin by reducing your portions. Try to eat with others rather than alone — eating alone leads to eating more, and there is less in solitary meals. The more people sharing a plate, the more descends, and the less food each person needs. Sheikh Khadir, when he returned to Mauritania, was once asked what had struck him most about life there. Among the things that shocked him most, he said, was that everyone ate from separate plates. When he described this to people back home, they were genuinely baffled — they simply could not imagine it. He said he embarrassed himself repeatedly, because a large communal plate would be set down and he would start eating from it, not realizing that people were waiting to serve themselves small portions onto their own dishes.

So eat together. There is in it. Aim for two meals a day if you can manage it. If you cannot, at the very least avoid heavy meals — eat what is enough, and stop. And keep in mind: the higher the quality of the food, the less of it you need. Part of the reason people here eat such enormous quantities is that the food is nutritionally poor. I am confident that in a typical American restaurant, the single serving placed in front of one person would feed ten people in West Africa. Ten people. And most diners here clean their plates.

So, you know, if the food is good, you'll need less of it. If the food is poor — empty calories, fast food, that sort of thing — you'll eat more and still feel unsatisfied. By good food and bad food I mean genuinely nutritious food: wholesome grains, vegetables, things like that. I wouldn't set foot in a fast food restaurant myself. Even if it's a McFish burger or whatever it is, I'd rather skip it. I might even say the cardboard box it came in is more nutritious. Throw the hamburger out — at least cardboard has roughage.
. If you want to bring the heart to life, give some time to the night. They say even two is enough. Sheikh Muhammad Ali ibn Malik said: never abandon, even if it is only two.

Sheikh Abdul Khadim, adds that in this age, when so many people find these practices difficult, it is far worse to do it sporadically than to do it modestly but consistently. One night you get up and pray ten with long and spend f an hour or more — and then the next night nothing, and the night after that nothing. It is far better to get up just five minutes before and pray two, every single night without fail. Make it a habit. Give some prayer to the night, do it consistently, and you will see results. A little here and a little there produces nothing. Ahmad Zarruq compared it to drilling a hole — a little bit here, a little bit there, and you will never strike water.
So give some portion to prayer. A few things about the prayer itself.

When the Prophet arrived in Medina, 'Abdullah ibn Salam — may be pleased with him, the rabbi who embraced Islam — narrated that the Prophet gave a khutbah after descending upon Quba. He said: O people, spread peace — greet one another with peace. Feed people. And pray in the night when others are sleeping. You will enter without any difficulty.

Just look at how straightforward that is. — spread peace. Do not be a cause of division. Be someone who unifies, who brings people together. — feed people. Be generous. When you feed someone, you are showing you care about them. So: spread peace, be concerned about others — and then tend to your own soul. Correct yourself. If you do those things — and that is a: if you do those things, that is the condition.. That is all. If every one of us took that single and made it our practice, that is a guarantee from the Messenger of that we will enter Paradise.

They said of one man who did some questionable things during the day but prayed at night: — it will eventually stop him, if he keeps at it. On the other hand, there is another, quite frightening, about a woman who prayed at night and gave but was cruel to her neighbors. — she used to treat her neighbors badly. And the Prophet said:. She is in the Fire. And it is a. Then of another person, they said: he does not pray at night, he does not give, he does not do these other things — — but he is good to his neighbors.. He will enter.

So you can pray all night if you like — but without good character, it counts for very little. Keep things in perspective. Tahajjud is immensely important, and has encouraged it for all believers. He says: — And from the night, spend a portion of it in as a, a voluntary act. Perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station. So this practice helps purify the heart.

And says of the believers: — they lift their sides from their beds at night when they would far rather sleep. Sleep is something the loves. We all love sleep. And that is precisely why restraining the from sleep — in moderation — is spiritually powerful. Not all night. You do not want to push yourself into a sleepless psychotic state. You do not deprive yourself entirely. Keep it within reasonable bounds.

In the same way, when they speak of hunger as a discipline, they do not mean the emaciated ascetic whose spine is visible — the image people call the starving Buddha, that famous statue. That is not our tradition. The point is to learn to govern the food-driven. The same applies to night prayers: you do not spend the entire night in prayer. There was a ta'ifa among the who spent a great deal of the night in prayer — not all of it, but a great deal. According to al-Raghib al-Isfahani, a ta'ifa is fewer than a thousand, so it was a number of the who sustained this, though not all of them.

Consider the well-known about the man the Prophet said was a man of Paradise. One of the followed him for several days and observed nothing remarkable. So he asked him directly: what are you doing? The man replied: all I know is that every night before I sleep, I make sure there is no rancor in my heart toward any Muslim. He was not praying at night, was not fasting, was not doing anything outwardly exceptional. Not all the prayed through the night.

But says of a group among them: — in one reading, they would not sleep at night; in another reading — they slept only a small portion of the night. Both readings are valid. The point is that for some among them, this was their particular practice.

For us, I think what is rational and reasonable is a steady, consistent practice — something regular. Shaykh Abdullah al-Haddad advises that given the nature of this age, it is good to recite the shorter that carry great reward. I mentioned last night the line: — when your life is drawing toward its end, start doing as much as you can. He actually recommends even just reciting ten times in short to accumulate great reward.

So even short count. If your practice is to pray some portion of the night and you happen to oversleep until just before, it is still permissible and acceptable to pray those as before your prayer — as long as you will not miss itself and as long as there is still some darkness before the sets in. You can easily pray ten with and proper in seven or eight minutes — they will not be rushed, they will be sound, and you can complete them in ten minutes or so. A minute per rakaat is quite manageable.

For women who cannot pray at certain times, it is perfectly acceptable to get up in the night and read something beneficial, or to meditate, or to make. You can recite in every rakaat. The that carry particular benefit — — those are the the Prophet used frequently. is another. He recited often. as well. And it is not a to recite the same surah in every rakaat of a voluntary prayer.

You shouldn't make it a regular practice, and there is some about this. The Shafi'is, I believe, would permit it, while the Malikis would consider it a. So be careful — for some imams it may be a, for others it may be acceptable. For Imam Malik, it is a to recite at every Maghrib prayer, whereas Shaykh Abdullah al-Haddad, in one of his treatises, mentioned that it was a good thing to do, and there is a indicating that one of the did exactly that. So you have to be a little careful with these matters.

There is also the about Sayyidina Abdullah ibn Umar, may be pleased with him. The Prophet once walked past him and said — "What an excellent man — if only he would spend some time at night in prayer." The scholars have clarified that this is not simply a compliment; the statement contains the word, a particle of wishing, as in. What the scholars took from this is that a person can still be a good person even without praying at night — like Abdullah ibn Umar — but how much better would he be if he did? The believer who hears that desires perfection. And so, when Abdullah ibn Umar heard those words — and he himself is the narrator of the, which he related to his son — he never abandoned again after that.

The scholars also drew from this that it is permissible to praise someone who will not be made conceited by that praise. The Prophet knew that Abdullah ibn Umar would not hear those words and think, "I'm already excellent, so I don't need to pray at night." Rather, it spurred him on to do more — which is exactly what happened.

Then there is the well-known of Aisha, which is a, in which she describes how the Prophet would pray so long at night that his feet would crack and become slightly swollen. What the physicians call venous stasis — when you stand for extended periods, blood can pool in the feet and cause mild edema. This is why people who are on their feet all day, such as nurses, often wear compression stockings to help the blood return upward. It happens to many people.

So Aisha said, ", why do you do this when your Lord has forgiven you everything — past and future?" And he replied, "Should I not be a grateful servant?" In other words, that very fact should make me want to show even more gratitude. Worship, then, is a way of expressing gratitude to. The scholars say this shows that one of the greatest ways to give thanks for the of is to do some night work —. And they say: — whoever seeks high things stays awake at night.

For students especially, the night is the best time to study. If falls at a particular hour, divide the night from Maghrib onward into six equal parts. Each part, in a twelve-hour night, would be roughly two hours. The last sixth of the night — the final two hours before — is the best time for. If we take, for simplicity, Maghrib at six p.m. and at six a.m., then four a.m. to six a.m. would be that optimal period. That said, any prayer after Isha counts as, and some scholars say even after Maghrib.

For people who find it genuinely difficult to rise in the early morning — those with what the tradition calls a "heavy liver," meaning a slow constitution — it is perfectly valid to pray some before going to bed. You should do something in the night hours. Interestingly, many people find it easier to wake up around three or four in the morning than right before, because the sleep immediately before is recognizably the heaviest sleep of the night. This is a from, and it also corresponds to what science tells us: cortisol levels in the brain are at their peak at that time. Ibn Ata'illah said the wisdom in this is that wants you to be able to pull yourself out of sleep precisely when it is most difficult to do so.

As for the number of: eight and ten are both established by, and I was told ten is the best. You pray two by two — two, four, six, eight, ten — and it is better done after Isha, unless you are someone who by nature rises every night without fail, in which case you may wait. Sayyidina Abu Bakr, who was very strong in his spiritual practice and certainly prayed the night prayer, used to pray before he went to bed.

What if you are staying up late — do you have to sleep first and then get up? No, you don't have to. Obviously it is better to sleep and then rise, because the Prophet said that was the best way — the way of Dawud, peace be upon him, who would sleep for a portion, rise for a portion, sleep again, and rise again. That is harder on the self than simply staying up, and he maintained that practice just as he maintained his fast of every other day. It is true — real mastery over the — because it is genuinely difficult to fall asleep and then get up again.

And never forget — — that is always nearby. — he ties three knots on your head while you sleep, in the unseen world, and whispers — "You have a long night ahead of you, just relax." In winter especially, this is all too convincing. Those three knots are heavy. The Prophet said that if you wake up and recite the of waking — — the first knot is loosened. If you get up and make, the second knot is loosened. And if you then pray, the third knot is loosened and you are freed entirely.

The Prophet was also asked about a man who slept straight through until morning without praying — and the fact that the asked about it shows this was not their norm. He said — "That is a man in whose ears urinated.". Anyone who does not pray the night prayer has using his ear as a toilet. We should not want that. The way out is simply to do something — get up in the night, pray even a few for.

Some of the scholars said this should be understood — literally — that literally urinates in the ear. And the principle in Islamic jurisprudence is that — the literal meaning is not set aside for a metaphorical one unless there is a necessity to do so. Some scholars found no such necessity and took it literally. Others interpreted it metaphorically, saying it means deprives that person of all the good that comes from spending part of the night in worship..
Can you remind us of the? — Praise be to the One who brought me back to life after He caused me to die, and to Him is my return.

There is also the practice of reciting the closing verses of upon waking. I spent many nights in 's tent, and every single night he would get up — usually four, sometimes five hours before — and he would wake you with those verses: — and I can still hear his voice reciting them., give us. It is all from — the ability to do these things is itself a gift from Him.

What prevents us from — what blocks it — is, eating what is, and similar violations. These are what close the door. This is a gift from, and those who have experienced it and then lost it know that when they had it, it truly felt like a gift, and when it was taken away, it felt like a punishment. So make, ask to restore it, and He will.

The people of the used to hold themselves to such rigorous that whenever something afflicted them they could trace the cause. One scholar said, "I once said something about someone that I should not have said, and I was deprived of for forty days because of it." They could see the direct connection between cause and consequence. Another scholar said that near the end of his life he went bankrupt, and he realized it was the result of something that had happened forty years earlier — he had once said to a man, "," meaning "you bankrupt one," and he understood that had given him exactly what he had called that other man. As the saying goes, the good actions of the righteous are the bad actions of those who are near to — meaning what is an ordinary slip for most people carries far greater weight for those whose hearts are refined.

On the question of: do not pray the twice. Witr should be the last prayer of the night — that is the correct practice. It is perfectly valid to pray additional prayers after, but should come last. So if you go to bed early, it is better to pray your before you sleep, since should be completed before. If you wake up and forgot to pray it, you can still make it up after, but it is better done before. In the, is; in the other, it is a — a strongly emphasized.

The and should be prayed before you go to bed. Then if you rise during the night, do not repeat the; simply pray in pairs — two by two, as the says. You do not pray four together; you pray two, then two.

If you are asking whether you can do after — yes, you can. The preferable practice is to delay the so that it is the last prayer of the night. That is the ideal. But put it this way: if you are as certain as one can reasonably be that you will wake up before, then it is better to delay your. If your consistent, reliable practice is to wake up f an hour or an hour before and pray — and you are confident in that pattern — then it is better to delay. If, on the other hand, you are not consistent in waking up, then it is better to pray your before you go to sleep.
And if you do wake up during the night before, you pray your without ending with, since you have already prayed it and there is only one in the night.

— Ingrizi nahi malum hai. That's all the Urdu I know. There is an Afghani joke along these lines. An American traveled to Afghanistan having heard that the country was home to great spiritual teachers and saints. He wanted to find the greatest of them. So he approached an Afghani man and asked, the way Americans do — assuming everyone speaks English — "Who is the greatest spiritual teacher in Afghanistan?" The man replied, "Nami fahman." So the American went around asking after Nami Fahman, treating it as a name.

At some point a funeral procession passed by, and he saw a crowd watching solemnly. He went up to one of the Afghans and asked, "Who just died?" The man replied, "Nami fahman." Nami fahman, of course, means "I don't understand" in Persian.

On another point — about taking things easy and not driving yourself into the ground — Shaykh Habib said in that you should travel the path with ease toward yourself. You need yourself to complete the journey. Your horse has to carry you to where you are going, so you treat your horse well. Do not wear it out to the point where it cannot carry you any further. He is not saying be lazy — he is saying do not exhaust yourself so completely that you lose the capacity to continue.

The goal is to move along the path with yearning. If you are not too hard on yourself, your self will actually begin to do these things. If you try to stay up the whole night, it is too much for the self. If you try to stay up f the night, it is still too much. The self loses energy and gives up entirely. But if you start small, something shifts — you begin to taste the sweetness of it, you feel the benefit, and you start to want it. The self begins to look forward to it. That is the point he is making.

And then he says: two prayed by a lover are better than a thousand prayed without love. If you pray two with — with genuine longing, with a real desire for 's pleasure — will love it. But if you are going through the motions thinking, "I have to do this, it is important, I must," with no love behind it — there is no love there. The action is driven by an idea in your head, not by your heart. The whole point is that all of this should arise from a yearning for, as a from.

And then he says: — silence. One of the diseases he addresses is lust for speech — — which is, for most people, a deeply ingrained drive. The Prophet said — whoever is given silence as part of his nature has been given wisdom. There is wisdom in silence itself, simply in being silent. Even an ignorant person, if he is given the gift of silence, possesses a kind of wisdom — because at the very least, if you are ignorant, silence keeps you from making a fool of yourself.

If you have something to say, speech is better than silence. If you have nothing to say, it is permissible — — but there is no benefit in it. And if that permissible speech amounts to casual pleasantries — how are you, where have you been — that is fine.
But if it turns to "did you hear about so-and-so," it slides toward either or. Learning to govern the tongue is a serious discipline.

Imam al-Shafi'i said that whenever he was in a gathering and felt moved to speak, he would first look inward and ask himself whether he was speaking out of a desire of the — to prove a point or display his knowledge. He would check whether he was content for someone else to say the very same thing. If he could honestly say yes, he would speak. If not, he would stay silent, as a for his. He also said that whenever he entered a debate, he would make that cause the truth to appear on his opponent's tongue, so that he himself could submit to it. He had no wish to win — he would have preferred to lose, because losing would make him humble. That is a, that is a man.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, was the most reserved of people. When he spoke, he spoke the truth. He was not what is called. He said — the most distant of you from me, and the most distant to me on the Day of Judgment, are the and the. The companions recognized the other terms, but did not know, and he explained it as. is someone who speaks incessantly — — they simply never stop talking. He disliked the chatterbox. If you are teaching or saying something of use, that is another matter entirely. But speech for speech's sake is a waste.
Imam Malik, said of one of his students: — he is a fine man, except that he speaks a whole month's worth of words in a single day.

Then there is — reflection in solitude. means to be in a place with no one around, engaged in reflection. In English we call this meditation, and it is a genuine practice — not yogic, but simply sitting and meditating. Within the Islamic tradition there are various forms. One is, or contemplating the states of the hereafter: you sit and walk through the raising from the grave and the scenes of the Day of Judgment. Another is in the divine names: you move through them — — and reflect on each attribute. So in solitude benefits the heart.

Then there is — keeping company with the righteous. This practice is rooted in a Quranic injunction: — O you who believe, have of and be with the truthful ones. This is what is called in the Persian tradition: keeping good company with righteous people in order to purify the heart.
Imam Ibn 'Ata'illah says in the: — Do not take as a companion someone whose state does not lift you, and whose speech does not direct you toward.

Sidi Ahmad Zarruq notes in his commentary that this is not referring to spiritual masters — it is referring to the friends you spend ordinary time with. You should seek people who will elevate your state, not drag it down. And when they elevate yours, their own state rises too.

What this means in practice is that such people are in a good state with — a state of gratitude. When you are around people who are genuinely grateful, it becomes difficult to complain. They are saying, I feel truly grateful, has given us so much — and you find yourself sitting there unable to say, sorry, I can't agree, life is hard. They are in a different from you. So if you are the one in, do not keep company with the one in. And if you are the one in, seek out the one in, so that you may become like him. Do not drag him down — let him lift you up. That is the teaching.

And as for their speech directing you to: there are people who, if you did complain to them, would gently say — — if you try to enumerate the blessings of, you cannot count them; that applies to everyone. So perhaps instead of cataloguing your troubles, you might try counting his blessings. They help you shift your focus. And it is remarkable how a person's entire state can be transformed simply by sitting with someone who offers sincere and good counsel. A heart that was utterly dark and negative can be turned around entirely, because the effect was real and valuable — the person's perspective changes, and that is guidance.

That is what you want. And on this, Sidi Abu al-Hasan said: — whoever directs you toward this world has cheated you. If someone's entire counsel to you is about financial planning, acquiring property, securing your future in this life — that is a sign that he has cheated you, because you could die at any moment.

The example I like to use is this: imagine two salesmen come to you. The first says, "I have a house for sale. The only drawback is that it could disappear at any time — I cannot tell you exactly when, maybe fifty years from now, but it will be gone within seventy at the most, and it could vanish at any point before that." The second says, "I have another house. It will last forever and is guaranteed — but it is more expensive." Which one do you buy? Seriously — which one? Any person of sound intellect is going to buy the second one.
That is the. And you purchase it with your soul. The other house, you also purchase with your soul — but you buy it by destroying the soul, not by preserving it.

So: keeping good company. Then Sidi Abu al-Hasan also said that the one who tells you to rush and pile up deeds has merely exhausted you — if you believe you will reach through your deeds alone, you will wear yourself out. — but the one who shows you the path to has given you sincere counsel. That path is the contentment of. If you are content with, a small amount of action will be enough. If you are not, no amount of action will ever suffice.
And finally, he speaks of taking refuge — of returning to the One to whom all affairs return, since says that to all affairs return. Seeking refuge in is, above all else, the truest remedy.

This is why a scholar of the path says that the only real cure for all these diseases of the heart is to go before in a state of complete neediness — please, I need to change, and I need You to help me change — with a genuine sense of urgency. If that is the state a person is in, then, will help them change.

For my own part, I truly believe that my coming to Islam was the result of a state I entered before I was Muslim — a state of complete. I called on by the name I knew, which was God, and I simply asked: give me guidance, show it to me. I was in a state of utter neediness. Most of the people I have met who became Muslim will confirm something similar: that there was a moment of absolute — just show me what to do. And then the guidance opened up, and it became very clear.. After that it becomes easy.

I believe is merciful, and that where there is sincerity, even within a person's limited and imperfect understanding, that is enough. There is an apocryp story — and because it is apocryp, no is based on it, I want to be clear about that — but it carries a wisdom that has been told: about the Prophet Musa, encountering a man who is speaking to about wanting to wash His feet, give Him a massage, and tend to Him — a man who is an anthropomorphist without knowing it.

And Musa, moved by righteousness, rebuked the man and explained the true meaning of. Yet reminded Musa that he had been harsh, for the man had spoken those words out of love — he was simply ignorant. The right response to ignorance is to teach. So the point is that everyone is at the level where they are. Even the one bowing before an idol — that is his understanding; that is where he stands. This is why says:
— while you know it is wrong. Once knowledge reaches a person, that is when destroys him. If someone has no knowledge, and 's messenger has not yet reached him, will not punish him:
So if someone does not know Islam and is genuinely seeking guidance, that guidance comes.

He is saying that you must be like someone who is drowning, or like someone lost in a barren desert who sees no source of help except the Almighty God. This is precisely what happened to Yusuf Islam. I heard him describe it in a lecture: he was caught in the undertow at Malibu, being dragged out to sea — genuinely terrifying — and in that moment he called on God completely and promised: give me guidance and I will follow it, whatever you ask of me. That is the — the drowning man — with nowhere left to turn.

And then there is Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, whose guidance came on a boat carrying Abyssinian Christians. When the waves began to overwhelm the vessel and everyone feared they would drown, Ikrimah started calling on Hubal. The Christians on board laughed at him. They said: you are calling on an idol made of wood, sitting in Mecca, to save you out here? And in that moment it struck him — how absurd it was. He realized he could only call on. And entered his heart right there. That is the state of the drowning man. And the author says this is in fact the most beneficial state — the one that will truly help us. It must reach the point where you are like a man going under.

beneficial actions for purifying the hea.title: Beneficial Actions for Purifying the Heart

cues.text: Now, on the actions that purify the heart, he says:
As for the action most beneficial for purifying the heart, none surpasses the one that is consistent — even if it is small. This comes from the hadith:
The best actions are the ones maintained continuously, even if they are slight.

Think of it this way: if you take a coin and polish it hard with a few vigorous strokes, then set it down, versus taking the same coin and polishing it gently but without stopping — the second coin becomes bright and shiny in a way the first never will. One burst of effort cannot do what quiet consistency achieves over time. The heart works the same way. What encrusts it through accumulated wrong actions is not undone by one intense push. A little effort, maintained steadily, is what gradually breaks that crust away. That is why small deeds done consistently far outweigh large deeds done once.

The proof is in how the Companions conducted themselves. They were always consistent in their practices. The man who asked the Prophet about fasting every other day — the fast of Dawud — came to regret it in his old age. But the scholars took that very regret as evidence: the Companions held even voluntary practices so seriously that they would not abandon what they had taken upon themselves. It was not that the practice was obligatory — it was that they had committed to it.

And if you read the, you find that the Prophet used to fast so much that the Companions thought he never broke his fast — and then there were times when they thought he never fasted at all. He used to spend so much of the night in prayer that they thought he never slept — and then there were times when they thought he barely did any.

There is something very important to understand about the Messenger of Allah. He is the universal prophet — his being encompasses the possibilities of every good believer. So in him, every good believer has a model. And different believers are opened to different things. There are people for whom is not the door Allah opens for them. There are people for whom recitation of the Quran is not their particular opening — their opening may be in hadith. Others are opened through, not fasting. Others through fasting, not. Some through wisdom. It is very rare for anyone to be opened through all of them simultaneously.

This is why, when the Prophet described the different gates of paradise — the gate for the fasters, the gate for the — Abu Bakr asked: Can anyone enter through all of them? And the Prophet said: — yes, and I hope you are one of them. As they say, I hope he was. The point is: keep working. That applies to all of us.

So some people are given broad and wide-ranging. Imam Malik, for instance, wore fine clothes, used the best scents, burned — and to an outsider, especially among the ascetics, this looked extravagant. One of the wrote him a letter saying: I cannot believe your state. You eat the finest flour, you wear expensive clothes, the perfume alone must cost a fortune — you would do better giving all of that up and spending less time with people. He was, after all, teaching extensively in the.

So the was essentially telling Imam Malik: compared to me, you are in a bad state. This is what is called — essentially a kind of spiritual boasting. And Imam Malik wrote back an extraordinary letter. He said: — servant of Allah — Allah has opened for His servants many doors of goodness.

He then says: include action done in the absence of witnesses, and action done out of love for Allah or in awe of Him. So one of the things that benefits the heart is performing acts that no one else can see. Giving charity privately. Praying in a way that no one observes. This protects you from and and everything that flows from them.

There is a story — it was actually Fudayl ibn Ayyad, not Bishr al-Hafi — who was once walking down a street and overheard someone say: there goes a man who spends the entire night in prayer. When Fudayl heard it, he burst into tears and said: I cannot remember ever spending a single complete night in prayer. And then he said: how great is the honor Allah has bestowed on me by veiling me and making people think I am better than I am. That idea — of concealing one's state, of hiding — is the better path.

And then action done out of love: that is the highest. The scholars say there are two principal motivations. One is — fear — which, when it reaches the level of, becomes: awe of Allah's greatness, a profound sense of in the divine presence. The other is — love — born of Allah's mercy, yearning for Allah, doing things out of that longing. That is the highest motive, and the author tells you that the final is.

He also says that the purest actions are those of the — the one who is free of worldly wants, who does what he does seeking nothing in return, no thanks, no gratitude, not even reward in the. He does it solely for Allah's sake. That is the highest and best action for the heart. is not an outward condition — it is the absence of attachment within the heart. The is not like the Christian ascetic who wears rough clothing and practices flagellation. In Islam, the ascetic is the one for whom the world has no grip on the heart. That is why Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf was a, even though he was one of the wealthiest men in Mecca.

Then the author says that the actions of those who strive out of hope are higher and more exalted than those driven by fear alone. If fear is your only motivation, that is still valid — Allah tells us to have — but hope lifts the action higher. And the Prophet, is the — the beloved of Allah — and Allah loved him. That is the pinnacle: mutual love between the servant and his Lord.

He then says: particularly, action whose benefits extend to others. An action that purifies the heart is made greater when it reaches beyond the self. Charity does not only benefit your own soul — it benefits another human being. And in every creature that possesses a moist liver — that is, every living thing — there is reward. Water an animal and there is reward. Plant a tree and every creature that eats from it, for as long as that tree stands, earns you reward. All of these things are elevated precisely because they extend outward.

Then he speaks of fasting in relation to one's character. If you are someone who has poor control over his appetite — if gluttony is your weakness — then fasting is particularly powerful for you. It strikes at the root of that disorder. But for someone who already has reasonable control over his relationship with food, fasting is still good, yet it will not work the same transformation as it does on the one who genuinely needs to discipline that aspect of himself.

Similarly with the miser: for a generous person, giving in charity is natural. For someone who is stingy, giving out is a far greater struggle — and for that very reason, it carries more weight. The hadith on this is direct: the best is what you give when you are healthy, when you want to hold on to it, and when you fear poverty. That is when giving out really costs you something. That is the that truly rubs 's nose in it.

Then he says: you earn reward in proportion to your avoidance of wrong. And this brings up a related point. There are people in the who spent the better part of their lives in disobedience, then in old age made and began lecturing the young. But that person does not carry the same as the young person who had every opportunity and every impulse toward disobedience — and chose otherwise. The older person no longer has the energy for most of those wrongs anyway. comes more easily when the temptation is largely gone.

There is also a real danger in the opposite direction: the heart that has been in disobedience for decades sometimes becomes so encrusted that a genuine return becomes very difficult. And yet, many Muslims do make as they grow older. They reach forty, forty-five, and something shifts. In Tunisia, they say the year of responsibility is forty — because that is when the came to the Prophet. Which has given some people the mistaken impression that you can do whatever you like before forty. This is ignorance, pure and simple. And yet it has become a kind of cultural artifact in parts of the Muslim world — people who say: when I go to, I will grow my beard and become a proper Muslim. Some of them do come back changed. But these attitudes are a marker of how far we have drifted from our tradition.

What Allah loves is the young person who is raised up in obedience. — youth — the Arabs generally put between fifteen and thirty-five, some say up to forty. After forty you are no longer a; you are a, a man.

Then he says: and also the contribution of a miser — giving out of the best of his wealth, while he is in sound health, seeking the pleasure of Allah — all of these things purify the heart. Moreover, anything done with discretion and concealment is also purifying. And the best of endeavors is the one that purifies the heart. So the best thing you can do with your life is what is genuinely good for your heart.

Likewise — and this is the other side — the worst things are those that harden the heart, especially when a person persists in them or takes pleasure in them. The that enjoyed them: those are the things most destructive to the heart.

One thing that hardens the heart is speaking at length without mentioning Allah. This is recorded in the of Imam Malik. is reported to have said: do not sit in gatherings without remembering Allah, for a gathering in which Allah is not mentioned will harden the heart — and you will not even notice it happening. The hardening comes gradually, spiritually and even, one might say, physically — and you are unaware. But the more the tongue is occupied with remembrance of Allah, the softer the heart becomes. That is simply the reality. The more someone does, the more compassion flows from them, and the more they benefit.

Now this brings us to a truly important point. Allah says that a wrong action that produces in its wake a sense of shame and brokenness before Allah is better than an act of obedience that produces pride and arrogance in the one who performs it. And this is the secret of wrong actions — the wisdom concealed within them. Allah permitted us to stumble so that through the stumbling we might arrive at this state. The Prophet, said: if you did not commit wrong actions, I would fear for you something worse than wrong actions — namely, being pleased with yourself, admiring yourself, vanity, the feeling that you are something wonderful. That is worse.

Now, Sidi Ahmad Zarruq clarifies this so there is no confusion. He says the good of is in the very essence of, and the evil he is describing is what obedience results in when it goes wrong. So do not misread this as saying that there is such a thing as good or bad. is good. is bad. Full stop. What is being said is about the secondary results. If the secondary result of an act of obedience was arrogance — and the secondary result of a disobedience was — then in terms of what was ultimately produced, the was the better outcome. The obedience generated poison; the disobedience generated a return to Allah.

Think of people in America who commit terrible crimes, go to prison, and find their way to Allah there. That happens often. The disobedience was genuinely wrong. But it became part of the causal chain through which Allah guided them. It was not a good thing — but it resulted in a good thing. And that is what he is saying: a wrong action that results in humility is preferable to an obedience that results in arrogance, in terms of what they produce in the heart.

An atom's weight of a lofty inward action — such as contentment, or trust in Allah — is greater with Allah than mountains of outward deeds performed without any heart. And this is the same principle as:
Two prayed with love are better than a thousand prayed without it. Immeasurably better.
Then he mentions what Imam Sahnun, may Allah be pleased with him, said:
Leaving a single of what Allah has made is better than performing seventy thousand and. A is the smallest unit of currency in the Arabic tradition — a farthing, a penny.
And they also relate that Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq said there are four things whose very best still carries a kind of diminishment:
A debt, even if it is only a.

A daughter, even if she is Maryam — not because daughters are lesser than sons in worth, but because in that social context she lacks the physical strength and social protection a man possesses. And the word in Arabic, let us not forget, also means — physically strong, or strong in position..
Asking a question, even if it is only: which way do I go? There is a humility inherent in asking that is itself a small diminishment of the self — not a wrong thing, just an honest reality.
And being alone — even for a single night.
